- Key risk factors for another >18% surge include acute supply shortages (deficit of 60,000+ units in Madrid), persistent and possibly accelerating foreign investment, and the city’s global attractiveness. However, these bullish drivers are increasingly offset by worsening affordability, weak wage growth, signs of local demand fatigue (particularly among youth and domestic buyers), and some incremental policy/regulatory headwinds (end of Golden Visa, rent controls).
- The historical base rate for two consecutive years of >18% nominal growth in mature European cities is extremely low, with most experts citing mean reversion and market cycles tending to moderate after outsized gains.
- Policy interventions so far have not cooled prices materially, but mounting social and political pressure may lead to further action if affordability deteriorates, presenting a possible cap on runaway price appreciation.

Typical ‘no’ scenarios envision continued double-digit but sub-18% annual growth (10–15%), matching mainstream projections and the natural moderation after a previous year’s surge. ‘Yes’ scenarios are described as tail events—requiring renewed supply paralysis, a global capital influx, or new market shocks.

Probabilities assigned by experts for an >18% increase in 2025 cluster between 8% and 22%, with most between 12–20%, and no one considering such an outcome likely (i.e., all probabilities well below 50%).
